paths.title: How the Web Works
paths.summary: What actually happens between typing an address and seeing a page: requests and responses, the structure of an HTML document, and the rules that style it.
paths.subject: Web development

lessons.title: Requests and responses
lessons.summary: The browser asks, the server answers, and the status code says how it went.
objectives: Describe the request and response pair that fetches a page.
Read the status code of a response.
Name the method a browser uses to fetch a page.

sections.heading: A conversation, not a broadcast
sections.body: A browser does not receive pages on its own. It sends an HTTP request to a server and waits for an HTTP response. The response carries a status code, some headers describing the content, and usually a body containing the page itself.

sections.heading: What happens when you open a page
steps: The browser turns the domain name into an IP address.
It opens a connection to that address and sends an HTTP request.
The server handles the request and replies with a status code and a body.
The browser reads the HTML and requests the images, styles and scripts it mentions.

sections.heading: A request and its response
sections.code:
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<!doctype html>
<title>Example</title>

sections.heading: Status codes worth knowing
rows: OK: the request succeeded and a body follows.
Moved Permanently: the resource now lives at another address.
Not Found: the server has nothing at that address.
Internal Server Error: the server failed while handling the request.

sections.body: A 404 is an answer, not a broken connection. The server responded successfully and told the browser that the resource does not exist.

checks.prompt: Which status code means the server could not find the requested resource?
checks.explanation: 404 means Not Found. A 500 means the server itself failed, which is a different problem.

checks.prompt: An HTTP response can carry a body containing the page itself.
checks.explanation: The response body is where the HTML, image or other content arrives.

checks.prompt: Which HTTP method does a browser usually use to fetch a page? Type one word.
checks.explanation: GET asks for a representation of a resource without changing it.

lessons.title: The structure of an HTML page
lessons.summary: Elements, attributes, and the difference between the head and the body of a document.
objectives: Recognise an element, its tag name and its attributes.
Say what belongs in the head and what belongs in the body.
Explain how a page gets its title.

sections.heading: Elements describe the structure
sections.body: HTML marks up content with elements. An element starts with a tag name in angle brackets and usually ends with a closing tag. Attributes sit inside the opening tag and add information, such as lang="en" on the html element.

sections.heading: A complete, if small, document
sections.code:
Hello

A paragraph of text.

sections.body: The head holds information about the page, such as its title and character set. The body holds what the visitor actually sees.
Text placed directly in the head does not appear on the page. Only content inside the body is displayed.

checks.prompt: Which element holds the content a visitor sees?
checks.explanation: The body contains the displayed content; the head describes the document.

checks.prompt: What does an attribute such as lang="en" describe?
checks.explanation: Attributes configure an element. lang tells the browser which language the content is written in.

checks.prompt: Which element sets the text shown in the browser tab? Type the element name only.
checks.explanation: The title element in the head supplies the text for the tab and for bookmarks.

lessons.title: Styling with CSS
lessons.summary: Selectors choose elements, declarations change how they look, and small mistakes change what is selected.
objectives: Read a CSS rule as a selector plus declarations.
Match element, class and id selectors to the elements they target.
Spot a selector that targets the wrong thing.

sections.heading: Rules select, then declare
sections.body: A CSS rule has a selector and a block of declarations. The selector chooses which elements the rule applies to, and each declaration sets one property to a value.

sections.heading: Two rules
Selector shapes
rows: Every element whose class attribute contains note.
The element whose id is main.

sections.body: A class selector needs a leading dot. Writing note { } looks for a <note> element, not for an element with class="note".

checks.prompt: .note selects every element whose class attribute contains note.
checks.explanation: The dot marks a class selector, and an element can carry several classes.

checks.prompt: Which selector matches the element with id="main"?
checks.explanation: An id selector starts with a hash: #main.

checks.prompt: Which selector matches every paragraph element? Type the selector.
checks.explanation: The element selector p matches every paragraph, so p { } styles all of them.
